overview: Mosaic is the world's leading producer and marketer of concentrated phosphate and potash crop nutrients, serving customers in approximately 40 countries. It is the second-largest integrated phosphate producer globally (mining rock in Florida, Brazil and Peru and processing it in Florida, Louisiana and Brazil), is typically among the top four global potash producers (mining in Saskatchewan and New Mexico), and is the leading fertilizer production and distribution company in Brazil through its Mosaic Fertilizantes segment. Operations are organized into three reportable segments -- Phosphate, Potash and Mosaic Fertilizantes -- supplemented by distribution businesses in China and India and a minority equity stake in Saudi Arabia's Ma'aden.

business_model.summary: Mosaic is a vertically integrated commodity producer that mines phosphate rock and potash and converts them into concentrated crop nutrients (DAP, MAP, MOP, MicroEssentials, K-Mag) and animal feed ingredients, sold largely as global commodities priced off delivered/benchmark price plus the cost of key inputs (ammonia, sulfur, natural gas). Revenue is transactional and highly cyclical, tied to global agricultural planting seasons (spring/fall) rather than recurring. Brazil operations (Mosaic Fertilizantes) also blend and distribute purchased nutrients, acting as a resale/distribution outlet for Mosaic's own Phosphate and Potash output as well as third-party nitrogen products.

revenue_streams.name: Phosphate segment
revenue_streams.trend: volatile - FY2026 YTD net sales up on higher prices despite steep margin compression

revenue_streams.name: Mosaic Fertilizantes (Brazil)
revenue_streams.trend: declining - volumes down sharply on Araxá idling/divestiture and credit-constrained Brazilian demand

revenue_streams.name: Potash segment
revenue_streams.trend: stable to modestly declining - volumes down on Carlsbad sale and mine downtime, prices firmer

business_model.customer_type: B2B - wholesale distributors, retail chains, cooperatives, independent retailers, national accounts, blenders and farmers; no meaningful direct-to-consumer business
business_model.geographic_mix: FY2026 YTD net sales: Brazil ~35%, United States ~33%, Canada ~14%, other foreign countries ~19% (by customer location); approximately 64% of FY2025 net sales were derived from customers outside the U.S.

competitive_position.market_position: Second-largest integrated phosphate producer globally (~10% of world annual phosphate production, ~72% of North American concentrated phosphate production); typically a top-four global potash producer (~12% of world annual potash production); largest fertilizer producer/distributor in Brazil (~17% of Brazil fertilizer shipments, ~73% of Brazilian concentrated phosphate production)

moat_factors.description: Owns its own Florida and Peruvian (Miski Mayo, 75% interest) phosphate rock reserves, giving a structural cost advantage over non-integrated phosphate producers that must buy rock on the open market

Saskatchewan (Esterhazy, Belle Plaine, Colonsay) and historically New Mexico (Carlsbad, sold 2026) reserves with multi-decade mine lives and Canpotex export pooling (36.2% entitlement) provide scale and logistics advantages in international markets

Owns port, warehouse and blending infrastructure across North America, Brazil, Paraguay, China and India -- unlike many competitors who lack their own distribution -- supporting economies of scale, transportation efficiency and market intelligence
Largest phosphate rock producer and blender in Brazil with mines/plants close to the world's largest fertilizer-consuming farm base, though this is now being pared back (Araxá divestiture)
U.S. countervailing duty orders on Moroccan and Russian phosphate imports (2021, under litigation) partially shield North American phosphate pricing

weaknesses: Pure commodity producer with essentially no pricing power or product differentiation beyond niche performance products (MicroEssentials, Aspire)

Heavily exposed to volatile, often supply-constrained input costs (sulfur, ammonia, natural gas) that can swing gross margin from strongly positive to negative within a quarter, as seen in Q3 2026 (Phosphate segment posted a $147.8M quarterly gross margin loss)

State-owned/subsidized competitors (China, Russia, Morocco, Belarus) can have access to cheaper feedstock, looser environmental standards, and may accept lower returns for political/employment reasons
Significant minority (non-controlled) stakes -- Ma'aden, Miski Mayo, Canpotex -- limit Mosaic's control over capacity, dividends and cash repatriation
Shrinking/optimizing Brazil footprint (Araxá divestiture, Patrocínio idling) reduces scale in a core growth market

growth_drivers: Long-term secular demand growth from rising global population, income growth and protein-rich diets, particularly in China, India, Brazil and other developing regions

Structural phosphate and potash supply tightness driven by geopolitical disruptions (Strait of Hormuz tensions curbing sulfur/ammonia flows, Kazakhstan sulfur export restrictions, Russia-Ukraine war effects on fertilizer and raw material trade) supporting higher realized crop nutrient prices

Portfolio optimization/capital discipline: divesting lower-return Brazilian assets (Araxá, Patrocínio, Taquari potash, idled Patos de Minas mine, Carlsbad potash mine, Kronau land) to focus capital on core low-cost Saskatchewan potash and Florida/Louisiana phosphate assets
MicroEssentials, Aspire and K-Mag performance/specialty products carry premium pricing versus commodity DAP/MAP/MOP
Mosaic Biosciences platform (biologicals) leveraging the existing distribution network for incremental, higher-margin sales
U.S. countervailing duty protection on Moroccan/Russian phosphate imports supports North American phosphate pricing
Potential easing of sulfur/ammonia constraints into 2027, which management flagged as a tailwind to margins once lower-cost sulfur contracts flow through inventory

business.description: Crop nutrient prices and volumes are historically cyclical with long periods of oversupply followed by shortage; Q3 2026 Phosphate segment swung to an operating loss despite higher selling prices because input costs rose even faster
High fertilizer prices can cause farmers to delay purchases; in 2026 management cited customer affordability challenges and reduced global phosphate demand
Limited customer credit availability in Brazil and competition from lower-concentration Chinese phosphate imports have pressured Mosaic Fertilizantes volumes and margins
Mosaic extends and guarantees customer financing, especially in Brazil, exposing it to customer default risk tied to weather, crop prices and local credit conditions

financial.description: Net interest expense rose ~27% YoY for the nine months ended September 2026 after $2B of new senior notes issued in August 2026 and a $500M term loan; long-term debt (incl. current maturities) stood at ~$5.4B at September 30, 2026 vs. cash of only $272.6M

Primary FX exposures are the Brazilian real and Canadian dollar; US dollar-denominated liabilities held by Brazilian/Canadian entities and real-denominated loans held by US entities create transaction gains/losses that swung from a $301M FX gain in 9M-2025 to a $36.5M gain in 9M-2026
Inventory carried at net realizable value; falling product prices (lagging falling raw material prices) have historically forced write-downs

financial.risk: Impairment risk on non-core assets and investments
financial.description: 2025-2026 saw impairments on Carlsbad ($191M), Taquari ($66M) and Araxá ($233M) disposal groups; Mosaic also holds a mark-to-market equity stake in Ma'aden that swung from large unrealized gains in 2025 to an $11M unrealized loss in 9M-2026

regulatory.risk: Florida/Louisiana environmental and phosphogypsum stack regulation
regulatory.description: Stringent EHS laws (CERCLA, RCRA consent decrees, FDEP/EPA water management rules for phosphogypsum stacks) require significant financial assurance (RCRA Trusts, ~$751M fair value at Sept 2026) and could raise compliance costs or restrict operations
A federal court decision invalidated Florida's assumption of Clean Water Act Section 404 dredge-and-fill permitting authority, potentially complicating and delaying mine permit renewals

U.S. tariffs on Canadian potash (25% imposed Feb 2025, currently exempted under USMCA-origin rules) could be reinstated and trigger Canadian retaliation; countervailing duty orders on Moroccan/Russian phosphate remain under litigation and could be reversed

Evolving GHG and climate disclosure rules in the EU, California and potentially the SEC could raise compliance costs, though the SEC's own climate rule is currently in abeyance and the U.S. withdrew from the Paris Agreement in January 2025

macro.description: Middle East conflict/Strait of Hormuz tensions and Kazakhstan sulfur export restrictions drove sulfur costs up 163% YoY in Q3 2026 (to $715/long ton), directly causing the Phosphate segment's quarterly operating loss; management guided Q4 2026 sulfur costs in COGS to $800-$850/ton before an expected easing in 2027

macro.risk: Russia/Belarus sanctions and export policy shifts
macro.description: Partial easing of U.S. sanctions on Belaruskali/BPC in 2026 has allowed small test shipments of Belarusian potash to the U.S., a potential long-term supply/pricing risk to Canpotex-marketed volumes, though logistics currently limit volumes
Chinese government export restraints/taxes on phosphate and potash can swing global supply; competing low-concentration Chinese phosphate imports have pressured Mosaic Fertilizantes margins in Brazil
Hurricanes (Gulf Coast facilities), drought and excess rainfall have repeatedly disrupted production, logistics (Mississippi River barge levels) and farmer application rates
Crop prices, farm income, biofuel policy and planted acreage directly drive crop nutrient demand and are outside Mosaic's control

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global phosphate supply is tightening into 2026-2027 due to sulfur/ammonia input constraints (Strait of Hormuz disruption, Kazakhstan sulfur export curbs) with management forecasting global phosphate shipments down ~20 million tonnes versus the prior year; potash markets are well-supplied and near pre-war production levels, with partial, logistically-constrained easing of Belarus sanctions limiting further price upside
macro_factors.cyclicality: High - crop nutrients are a classically cyclical commodity business with large swings in capacity utilization, pricing and margins across the agricultural planting cycle and global supply/demand balance
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate - working-capital-intensive, seasonal business with ~$5.9B of total debt as of Q3 2026 (including recent $2B senior notes issuance); higher rates raise financing costs and discount the value of long-dated mine assets

recent_developments.event: Net loss of $72.1M ($(0.23) diluted EPS) vs. net income of $411.4M a year earlier; Phosphate segment posted a $194M operating loss (vs. $102M profit) driven by sulfur costs up 163% YoY to $715/long ton; Potash operating earnings fell to $188M; Mosaic Fertilizantes posted a $22M operating loss

Issued $2.0B of new senior notes ($1.0B 5.350% due 2031, $500M 5.650% due 2034, $500M 5.900% due 2036); used proceeds to tender/redeem $1.4B of existing notes (recognizing a $13.1M loss on extinguishment) and repay a $500M term loan

Committed to divest the Araxá mining/chemical complex in Brazil and idled the related Patrocínio mine, recording ~$496M of combined impairment, write-off and idling costs for the nine months ended September 30, 2026

Completed sale of the Carlsbad, New Mexico potash mine for ~$20M plus $10M deferred consideration, narrowing Potash segment focus to Canadian (Saskatchewan) operations; recognized a further $6.2M impairment on finalization (total impairment on Carlsbad ~$191M)
Agreed to sell ~11,858 acres of land near Kronau, Saskatchewan for ~$36M (retaining mineral rights); transaction closed in Q4 2026 with a gain to be recognized then

Temporarily curtailed phosphate production at multiple North American and Brazilian facilities (including Bartow) in response to constrained, high-cost sulfur supply; Phosphate operating rate fell to 52% in Q3 2026 from 68% a year earlier; Brazil phosphate operating rate fell to 27% from 84%
Completed sale of the Taquari potash mine interest in Brazil (~$27M proceeds, ~$66M impairment) and closed a $900M bond offering ($500M 4.350% notes due 2029, $400M 4.600% notes due 2030)
Completed sale of the idled Patos de Minas phosphate mining unit in Brazil for $111M, recording a $94M gain

Multiple sell-side price-target cuts through 2026 (UBS to $19, Barclays to $22, CIBC to $22, Morgan Stanley to $26) and an RBC downgrade to Sector Perform, reflecting margin pressure from input costs, though consensus rating remains mixed Hold/Buy with average targets in the $22-$26 range

items.metric: Sulfur cost in cost of goods sold
items.notes: Reflects higher-cost sulfur purchased earlier in the year flowing through inventory; management expects this cost headwind to be the low point before easing as cheaper contracted sulfur reaches COGS in Q1 2027
Cut from prior expectations due to downtime/production issues at the Esterhazy, Saskatchewan mine

items.target: Q4 2026 expected to be the cyclical low point for earnings, with margin relief into Q1 2027
items.notes: Management attributes the near-term trough to the lag between high-cost sulfur purchases and their flow-through to cost of goods sold

items.target: Maintain investment-grade credit metrics; target liquidity buffer up to $3.0B; continue dividends; fund organic growth/strategic opportunities
items.notes: Per Q3 2026 10-Q Liquidity and Capital Resources discussion; $210.6M of dividends paid and $958.6M of capex in the nine months ended September 30, 2026 (down slightly from $1,009.8M in the prior-year period)

guidance.management_commentary: Management attributed the Q3 2026 loss primarily to a global sulfur supply shock (Strait of Hormuz tensions, Kazakhstan export restrictions) that pushed consumed sulfur costs up over 160% year-over-year, more than offsetting higher average selling prices for phosphate and potash. Mosaic responded by curtailing production at high-cost facilities in North America and Brazil, continuing to idle/divest lower-return Brazilian assets (Araxá, Patrocínio), and terming out debt via a $2 billion senior notes issuance to preserve investment-grade liquidity. Management expects global phosphate shipments to fall materially (management-cited estimate of roughly 20 million tonnes versus the prior year) and views Q4 2026 as the likely earnings trough before input-cost relief reaches the income statement in 2027.

bull_case: Structural phosphate and potash supply tightness from geopolitical disruptions (Strait of Hormuz, Kazakhstan sulfur curbs, Russia/Ukraine war effects) is pushing up global crop nutrient selling prices, with average phosphate and potash prices up double digits year-over-year even as near-term margins are squeezed

Vertically integrated, low-cost Florida/Louisiana phosphate rock and Saskatchewan potash reserve base provides a durable structural cost advantage versus non-integrated and higher-cost global competitors once input cost pressures normalize

Active portfolio optimization (divesting Araxá, Patrocínio, Taquari, Carlsbad, non-core Brazilian/Saskatchewan land) focuses capital on the highest-return core assets and should reduce capex and operating costs going forward
Management expects Q4 2026 to mark the cyclical earnings trough, with lower-cost sulfur contracts flowing through cost of goods sold and improving margins into 2027

Long-term secular demand tailwinds from global population growth, rising incomes and dietary shifts toward protein support multi-year crop nutrient demand growth, particularly in China, India and Brazil
bear_case: Pure commodity exposure with volatile, often unhedgeable input costs (sulfur, ammonia) can overwhelm pricing gains, as shown by the Phosphate segment's swing to a large operating loss in Q3 2026 despite higher selling prices

Rising leverage (~$5.9B total debt after the August 2026 $2B note issuance) and higher interest expense reduce financial flexibility just as operating cash flow has fallen sharply (9M-2026 operating cash flow down ~37% YoY)

Brazil business is shrinking and under pressure from credit-constrained farmer demand and competition from low-concentration Chinese phosphate imports, with the Araxá divestiture and Patrocínio idling removing meaningful production capacity and causing large one-time charges (~$496M in 9M-2026)
Partial easing of Belarus/Russia sanctions could gradually add potash supply to Western markets, capping potash price upside even as logistics currently constrain near-term volumes

Sell-side sentiment has deteriorated through 2026, with several analysts (UBS, Barclays, CIBC, Morgan Stanley) cutting price targets and RBC downgrading the stock, reflecting skepticism about near-term margin recovery
